profiles.meeting_scenario: A 30-minute troubleshooting meeting at a robotics software company about an internal report-based specification debugging toolkit used on GR(1) controller specs for an automated warehouse loading-bay system. Context: the overnight CI pipeline for the demo branch produced a 'clean' HTML debugging report for the loading-bay controller, but the subsequent synthesis job marked the spec unrealizable after a low-battery door-interlock update. Agenda: compare what artifact each person reviewed, determine whether the issue comes from the specification change, the report-generation pipeline, or stale preprocessing/caching, and decide what rerun or patch should happen before an afternoon customer demo. Expected outcome: agree on a concrete next diagnostic step and a short-term remediation path, while both participants believe they have aligned on what needs to be rerun and what counts as resolving the issue.

members.name: Priya Raman
members.expertise: Reactive synthesis, temporal logic specifications, GR(1) debugging workflows
members.background: Priya designed much of the team's report-based specification analysis flow and regularly supports controls engineers who write structured temporal-logic specs for warehouse subsystems.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve confidence in the report-based debugger as a low-effort first-line tool, suspects the discrepancy is caused by preprocessing or integration rather than a conceptual limitation, and is worried the demo team will stop trusting the formal methods workflow if the report appears misleading.
hidden_assumptions: When people mention 'the report', they mean the analysis of the normalized, fully composed GR(1) game after macro expansion, monitor lowering, and environment/system composition.
The relevant 'latest loading-bay spec' is the demo-branch version that already includes the support patch adding the sensor_clear fairness assumption alongside the door interlock change.
Autogenerated monitors and imported plant assumptions are part of the real spec for debugging purposes, even if engineers did not handwrite them.
A troubleshooting fix is only meaningful if the report helps an engineer see the cause of unrealizability or vacuity before running expensive synthesis.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: CI pipelines, build caching, synthesis job orchestration, internal verification tooling
members.background: Leo maintains the nightly verification pipeline, job templates, and report publication logic for several controller teams, with a focus on keeping analysis turnaround and compute usage manageable.
members.private_state: He wants a low-risk operational fix that keeps the nightly pipeline within its time budget, suspects the issue is localized to a recent spec edit or branch mismatch, and does not want to expand the expensive compose-and-lower stage unless absolutely necessary.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the report', they mean the published module-level HTML artifact generated from the handwritten controller clauses, with environment summaries reused from cache unless that cache is explicitly invalidated.
The 'door interlock change from yesterday' refers to the main-branch ticket commit associated with the Jira item, not the later demo-branch merge stack.
For reruns, 'full spec' usually means the full controller package target, not generated monitor artifacts or external plant-side contracts that live outside the module's source directory.
In practice, the issue is fixed once the branch goes green again and the synthesis/regression jobs complete for the demo timeline, even if the report remains as coarse as before.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the report' or say the report looked clean
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the debugging report over the normalized, fully composed specification after preprocessing, including environment assumptions and lowered monitors.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the published HTML report for the handwritten loading-bay controller module, generated with cached environment summaries and without necessarily reflecting the latest composed game.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one prominent report.html link in CI, so both naturally use the singular phrase 'the report' without restating pipeline internals; the surface agreement feels safe because each assumes the coverage boundaries are obvious.

misalignment_points.topic: Which spec revision 'the latest loading-bay change' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention the loading-bay change from yesterday or the latest spec
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of demo-branch commit 8f2c1a, where the door-interlock change is already combined with a support patch that adds the fairness assumption GF sensor_clear.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of main-branch commit c73de9 tied to the Jira ticket, where only the safety clause G(door_closing -> !forklift_in_bay) changed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both commits are associated with the same feature label and ticket, and in a short troubleshooting meeting it feels unnecessary to read out SHAs when everyone believes they are talking about the same change.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as rerunning the 'full spec'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to rerun the full spec
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means rerunning analysis on the composed top-level spec, including autogenerated request/ack monitors, imported plant assumptions, and the lowered GR(1) representation used by synthesis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means rerunning the loading-bay controller package target, excluding generated monitors and external plant-side contracts unless a separate compose job is explicitly requested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The target name used in tooling sounds comprehensive in both workflows, so 'full spec' appears self-explanatory even though each person's everyday boundary for the spec is different.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the issue to be 'fixed'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about being fixed today or resolving the issue before the demo
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 considers it fixed if the report-based debugger exposes the hidden contradiction or vacuity source clearly enough that an engineer could catch it before synthesis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 considers it fixed if the demo branch pipeline stops failing and synthesis/regression complete successfully within the nightly budget.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, teams often compress diagnosis quality and operational recovery into one word like 'fixed', and both participants are cooperative enough that the different success thresholds do not sound like disagreement.

turns.inner_thought: The overnight analysis over the normalized, fully composed GR(1) game for the demo branch should not have looked clean if synthesis later found unrealizability. I'm thinking of the demo-branch latest loading-bay spec at 8f2c1a, where the door interlock update is already combined with the support patch adding GF sensor_clear. If the report missed something there, I need to know whether preprocessing or integration drifted, because I do not want people concluding the report-based debugger is fundamentally unreliable.
turns.utterance: I wanted to start with the mismatch from overnight. The report looked clean on the loading-bay side, but synthesis still marked the demo branch unrealizable after the latest loading-bay change from yesterday. That combination is what worries me.

turns.inner_thought: I checked the published report.html tied to the loading-bay Jira ticket on main, which for me is the door-interlock commit c73de9. That artifact only covers the handwritten controller clauses, and it looked fine. If this is just a branch mismatch or a stale cache around the report job, I can fix it without expanding the expensive compose path.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I looked at the report.html attached to that loading-bay ticket, and from what I could see it only reflected the door-interlock change from yesterday. I didn't notice any obvious warnings there either.

turns.inner_thought: Interesting—if he's looking at the same latest spec I am, then the sensor_clear fairness assumption was already in and should have influenced the analysis context. That makes a 'clean' report even harder to reconcile with unrealizability. Maybe the support patch never made it into whatever artifact he checked, but I don't want to jump to that before we verify the pipeline path.
turns.utterance: That's why it stood out to me. The version I reviewed also had the sensor_clear fairness assumption merged in, so seeing the report come back clean was even more surprising.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, that reinforces my suspicion that she's expecting more coverage from the published HTML than it actually guarantees. In our pipeline, the report is generated off the controller module and can reuse a cached environment summary unless cache invalidation is triggered. So a clean report may just mean no local vacuity in the module-level clauses, not that the fully composed behavior is okay. I still want to keep this bounded to the cheaper path first.
turns.utterance: One thing to keep in mind is that the report can be pretty local in what it confirms. If the environment side got reused from cache, then 'clean' may only mean there wasn't any obvious vacuity in that slice, not that everything downstream stayed consistent.

turns.inner_thought: Right, which is exactly why we need the composed top-level analysis, with autogenerated request/ack monitors lowered and imported plant assumptions included. The contradiction could easily arise only after environment/system composition in the lowered GR(1) game. A module-only rerun won't tell us whether the debugger can expose the actual cause before synthesis.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think the next useful step is to rerun the full spec with the monitors lowered, because the contradiction may only show up once the plant handshake logic is in the picture.

turns.inner_thought: I can say yes to rerunning the full spec, but operationally I mean the full loading-bay package target first. That should be fast enough to fit this morning, and if it reproduces or clears, we may not need the costly compose-and-lower expansion. I definitely don't want to trigger the broader external-contract path unless we have to.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll rerun the full spec, but I'll start with the faster loading-bay package target so we don't pay for the expensive compose step unless the first pass still looks off.

turns.inner_thought: As long as today's fix preserves trust in the report-based debugging flow. If this ends with 'synthesis eventually tells you it's broken' while the report stays clean, the controls engineers will stop using the report as a first-line diagnosis tool. I need the fix to make the hidden contradiction or vacuity visible before anyone burns synthesis time.
turns.utterance: That's fine as a sequence. I just want to make sure that if we patch this today, the report actually points engineers to the unrealizable corner before they have to run synthesis.

turns.inner_thought: For me, success today is much more practical: if the demo branch goes green again and tonight's synthesis and regression fit inside budget, we've stabilized the situation enough for the customer timeline. We can improve report fidelity later if needed, but I don't want to promise pipeline expansion before the demo.
turns.utterance: Totally. For the demo timeline, though, if we can get the branch green again and have tonight's synthesis complete, I'd already count that as fixed enough for today.

turns.inner_thought: I should anchor this by comparing the demo-branch artifact against the earlier ticket branch. If the behavior changes exactly when the fairness patch plus interlock update lands, that will tell us whether the issue is in the latest loading-bay spec versus preprocessing around it. I'm still thinking of demo branch versus the earlier branch state around c73de9, though I assume Leo is tracking the same lineage.
turns.utterance: Could we also compare the demo-branch artifact against the earlier ticket branch? That should help isolate where the latest loading-bay spec started behaving differently.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—I'll regenerate the report with the cache path adjusted so the module artifact is fresh, then rerun what I consider the full loading-bay spec target. If that gets the branch back to green before lunch, we have a workable fix path for the demo. If not, I can escalate to the more expensive compose job afterward.
turns.utterance: Yep, that's workable. I'll regenerate the report after adjusting the cache path, and I'll rerun the full spec so we can confirm the fix path before lunch.
